notes.meaning: The psalmist calls on the people of Israel to listen closely to what he is about to teach. He speaks with deep care, like a father or a teacher sharing God's truth with those he loves. Because this message carries the commanding authority of God's instruction, it deserves their full and humble attention.

The speaker announces that he will teach deep lessons through ancient stories. These stories are called hidden things or dark sayings not because they are impossible to understand, but because they contain rich spiritual meaning that takes serious thought to uncover. The events of Israel's past are meant to serve as living parables to guide later generations.

The lessons being taught are not human inventions or novel ideas. They are dependable truths that earlier generations experienced firsthand and passed down through the community of faith. God's people heard these historical facts and knew with certainty that they were true.

God's people made a firm promise never to keep these sacred truths hidden to themselves. They took on the duty of telling the next generation about the Lord's worthy praise, His great power, and the miracles He performed. Passing down the story of what God has done helps young people learn to revere and worship Him.

God gave His written law and His covenant—a binding sacred agreement—to Israel, commanding parents to teach it diligently to their children. This chain of instruction was intended to continue without break, reaching boys and girls who were not even born yet. Each generation was expected to grow up, arise, and pass the exact same truth on to the next.

The main goal of teaching children God's deeds is so that they will place their whole trust in Him. Actively remembering what the Lord has done strengthens a person's faith and encourages regular obedience to His commands. Real learning moves beyond just knowing facts into daily, heartfelt confidence in God.

Faithful teaching is designed to break the tragic patterns of the past. The older generation had been stubborn and rebellious in the desert, wandering away from the Lord even after seeing His kindness. Children are warned not to copy the bad example of their ancestors, whose hearts were divided and unfaithful.

The warriors of Ephraim were well-equipped archers, but they retreated in fear when the battle arrived. Despite having the right weapons, they lacked the faith and courage needed to stand firm. Their failure on the battlefield pictures how easily people turn back from God when a real test comes.

The people broke their sacred covenant with God and refused to follow His commandments. The root cause of this failure was that they simply forgot the marvelous deeds He had shown them. Forgetting God's past mercies always opens the door to disobedience and ingratitude.

The writer reminds the people of the great miracles God performed before their ancestors in the land of Egypt, especially near the capital city of Zoan. God displayed His wonders right in the heart of Pharaoh's powerful nation so that everyone could witness them. These public displays of divine power left the nation without any excuse for doubting Him later.

God miraculously split the Red Sea so His people could walk straight through it. He made the raging waters stand upright like solid walls on either side to let them pass in safety. This rescue proved that even the wild forces of nature must obey the command of the Creator.

God personally led the tribes throughout their journey in the desert. During the day, a pillar of cloud gave them shade from the scorching sun, and at night, a pillar of fire provided light and warmth. This tender care showed that God never leaves His people to find their own way through the dark.

When the people were parched in the wilderness, God split hard rocks open to supply them with fresh water. The water did not come out as a few drops, but poured out in rushing torrents like deep rivers so the whole nation could drink. This miraculous supply revealed how rich and generous God is when meeting the needs of His people.

Even after drinking from the miraculous rock, the people continued to sin against the Most High God. Their complaining grew worse instead of better, showing that miracles alone cannot change a rebellious human heart. Instead of thanking the Lord for keeping them alive, they openly challenged His authority.

The people tested God in their hearts by demanding the specific rich foods they craved. God was already supplying wholesome bread to sustain their lives, but they wanted a luxury feast to satisfy their selfish desires. Demanding more than what is needed and dictating terms to God is an arrogant challenge to His wisdom.

The Israelites boldly spoke against God, questioning whether He could really set a full dining table in the dry desert. They admitted He had cracked open the rock to make water gush out, yet they still doubted whether He had enough power to give them bread and meat. This attitude showed how unreasonable unbelief is, since they accepted one impossible miracle while doubting another.

The Lord heard their insolent words and was filled with intense anger, sending fire among them as a warning judgment. His displeasure flared because they refused to believe His word or rely on His promise to protect and deliver them. Failing to trust God's salvation after seeing His past goodness is treated in Scripture as the root of all other sins.

Despite the people's stubborn doubt, God graciously commanded the skies above to open wide. He showered down manna like rain, providing daily food that is called heavenly grain because it came straight from the sky. This abundant supply showed that God's patience and mercy far surpassed the undeserving behavior of His people.
